Statistics Seminar Series

Refreshments at 3:30pm in MSB 4110 (Statistics Lounge)

Speaker:              Yuedong Wang (UC Santa Barbara)

Title:                      A Suite of S functions Implementing Spline smoothing Techniques

Abstract:              We present a suite of user friendly R functions for fitting various smoothing spline models including (a) non-parametric regression models for independent and correlated Gaussian data, and for independent binomial, Poisson and Gamma data;

(b) semi-parametric linear mixed-effects models;

(c) non-parametric nonlinear regression models;

(d) semi-parametric nonlinear regression models; and

(e) semi-parametric nonlinear mixed-effects models. The general form of smoothing splines based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces is used to model non-parametric functions. Thus these R functions deal with many different situations in a unified fashion. Well known special cases are polynomial, periodic, spherical, thin-plate and L splines, GAM, SS ANOVA, projection pursuit, multiple index, varying coefficient, functional linear and self-modeling nonlinear regression models.

This abstract is also posted on our website at: http://www.stat.ucdavis.edu/seminars/winter15/031215-wang.html

messages.body_plain:
Apologies for the large file, but it's the actual data I'm working with and I thought that would be worthwhile.

I really am not sure how to even get started. I've looked at FCA [factanal()], but it says it wants to convert the SNP values (A/A, T/T, G/G, C/C, -/- (NA), and Heterozygous) into some sort of numeric frame and I'm not sure that makes sense. The geneticist who normally does this uses filtering in Excel, and I thought we are doing this enough lately that a more computational method rather than relying on human pattern recognition (which is pretty good).

Any tips/pointers/direction?

Thanks,

Brandon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brandon,

Are the parents of the cross also genotyped?

If so, you want to recode the SNPs as being from one parent or the other.  For example, parent-A SNPs in the lines are set equal 1 and parent-B SNPs equal to -1.  That can be done in R with a simple function, and several folks on the D-RUG list can help you with the recoding.  Once that's done, and assuming you can place your SNPs (or the reads they came from) in a genomic context, you want to look for portions of the genome in which the 2 pools of lines in your Bulk Segregant population are fixed (or almost so) for opposite parent SNPs: one pool for parent-A SNPs and the other for parent-B SNPs.

To do so, take the recoded SNP genotypes of 1 of the 2 pools and calculate a running average per chromosome.  You can use functions in the "zoo" package or others to calculate a running average.  Your region(s) of interest containing your plausibly causative gene(s) will have a running average equal or near 1 or -1, depending on how you coded the SNPs and which of the 2 pools you're focusing on.

...you can then "drill" deeper into that portion(s) of the genome by taking a closer look at the local SNP genotypes and the putative functions of genes in that region(s).

Does that make sense?

HTH,
Dan.

messages.body_plain:
Oh, they're RILs.  No wonder you've only got homozygotes!  That makes it easier, provided you have the parental genotypes.

You want the genotype at the same SNPs for the parents of that hybrid.

Yep, you're missing some things.  You cannot run the running averages as I suggested without being able to assign the SNPs to the parents.

Without parental info you'll have to infer haplotypes and then go from there.  I could envision some ways to approaching this without parental info, but it's much easier with the parental info.  Worst case scenario, even genotype info. from 1 parent would allow for a qualitatively much much easier analysis.

You could use the correlation among all lines to start getting an idea as to which lines would likely share haplotype blocks and then go from there to start finding recombination breakpoints, etc.  I cannot quite think right now of a fully fleshed out way of analyzing this that could be coded, though.

If I were you, I would genotype one of the parents for the original hybrid with the same SNP chip  ...even if it's from some old sample hidden in a freezer.  Ask around for such a sample or seeds!

Actually, since it's a BSA, all you need is to find regions of the genome where your 2 pools have perfectly (or near so) differentiate genotypes.

If you haven't done a lot of biased selection of progeny in making the RIL lines, each pool of lines will have a mix of genotypes (roughly 50/50) at most SNPs not in the region of interest.  In the region(s) of interest each pool will have a run of SNPs at which they're all identical and different from the other pool.  It should be relatively easy to find these regions.

This is what I would do:
Divide the data frame into 2 subset data frames corresponding to the 2 BSA pools
convert genotypes to single letter factors; drop SNPs with hets if need be.  Each SNP is a factor column, and the lines are rows.
droplevels
find SNPs (i.e. columns) within each of the separate pools' data frames that have just 1 level
Find runs (i.e. consecutive) of SNPs with just 1 level in the 2 data frames.
Confirm that where (genome position wise) one pool has a run of 1 level columns the other one does too

Dan,

I think I got something that works.

I divided it like you said, but I left them as characters so I could compare the two reads and label Hets. I then took the most frequent read and subtracted the number of lines in that group (trait = 0 or trait = 1; they were not equal). I then created a new summary that labeled things that had fewer than 5 "discrepancies". This highlighted two places only, with one being isolated (random chance?) and another region with 6 hits. It's a start anyway. Thanks for the help.

Final working code for posterity:

BSA <- read.delim("SNPdata.txt", stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

#vector to store number of levels

# levelNum <- rep(0, ncol(BSA)-2)

# for (i in 3:ncol(BSA)) {
# levelNum[i] <- length(levels(factor(BSA[[i]])))
# }

# #gets rid of columns with only one level, only one genotype
# BSA <- BSA[-which(levelNum == 1)]

#loop over columns with genotyping information

for (i in 3:ncol(BSA)) {

#split genotype reads by /
markersplit <- strsplit(BSA[[i]], "/")
#store the two reads
read1    <- unlist(markersplit)[2*(1:length(BSA[[i]]))-1]
read2    <- unlist(markersplit)[2*(1:length(BSA[[i]]))  ]
#create variable for storing singular read
result <- rep(0, length(read1))
# loop over reads and store NA, Base, or Het
for (j in 1:length(read1)){
if (read1[j] == "-") {
result[j] <- "NA"
}
else if (read1[j] == read2[j]) {
result[j] <- read1[j]
}
else {
result[j] <- "Het"
}
}
#store result vector back into BSA data.frame
BSA[i] <- result
}

#split data.frame by Trait phenotype
trait1 <- BSA[BSA$Trait == 1, ]
trait0 <- BSA[BSA$Trait == 0, ]

#compute which base is read most often per marker and
# the number of times it is present minus the total number of lines in subset
maxbass0 <- apply(trait0[-c(1, 2)], 2, function(x) names(which.max(table(x))))
maxcount0 <- apply(trait0[-c(1, 2)], 2, function(x) table(x)[which.max(table(x))]) - nrow(trait0)

#compute which base is read most often per marker and
# the number of times it is present minus the total number of lines in subset
maxbass1 <- apply(trait1[-c(1, 2)], 2, function(x) names(which.max(table(x))))
maxcount1 <- apply(trait1[-c(1, 2)], 2, function(x) table(x)[which.max(table(x))]) - nrow(trait1)

#rbind results into one data.frame
BSAout <- rbind(maxbass0, maxcount0, maxbass1, maxcount1)

#uncomment to write out file
#write.table(BSAout, file = "BSAout.txt", quote=F, na  = "", sep = "\t", row.names=F)

#create variable to summarize data further
BSAsummary <- rep(NA, ncol(BSAout))

#loop over columns of BSAout and summarize results whether
# they are the same or different enough for further analysis
for (i in 1:ncol(BSAout)) {
# if they are the same base, it's monomorphic
if (BSAout[1,i] == BSAout[3,i]) {
BSAsummary[i] = 0
}
#not monomorphic
else {
# if one trait group is mostly Het, this isn't good either
if (BSAout[1,i] == "Het" || BSAout[3,i] == "Het") {
BSAsummary[i] = 1
}
#not monomorphic or Het
else {
# if more then 5 discrepancies then classify differently
if (as.numeric(BSAout[2,i]) < -5 || as.numeric(BSAout[4,i]) < -5) {
BSAsummary[i] = 2
}
#not monomorphic or het and fewer than 5 discrepancies between geno-/pheno-type
else {
BSAsummary[i] = 40
}
}
}
}
#print details and look for 40s (Colt 45?)
BSAsummary

Here I’m using dplyr syntax to do this. dplyr works well on data.tables. You could do this in data.table’s own syntax but I’m screwing it up trying that. dplyr’s syntax is a little more verbose but rather clear.
library(data.table)
library(dplyr)

# rebuilding the example data
# Next time you can make sure we have the same data by pasting the results of
# dput(hospitalization[1:3,]) into your email
hospitalization = as.data.frame(rbind(c(100567, 0700, 51881, 19, 0052),
c(100568, 9847, 0300, 4, 4011),
c(100569, 3187, 3481, 2, 2939)))
names(hospitalization) = c("hospitalization_no", "diagnosis1", "diagnosis2", "LOS", "diagnosis3")

hospitalization$diagnosis1 = as.character(hospitalization$diagnosis1)
hospitalization$diagnosis2 = as.character(hospitalization$diagnosis2)
hospitalization$diagnosis3 = as.character(hospitalization$diagnosis3)
organ_dysfunction = c("5185", "51881", "51882", "51884", "51885", "78609", "7991", "0967", "09671", "09672", "4275", "4580", "4582", "4588", "4589", "78550", "75851", "75852", "75859", "7963", "580", "5804", "5800", "58081", "58089", "5809", "584", "5845", "5846", "5847", "5848", "5849", "570", "5722", "5733", "2866", "2869", "2873", "2874", "2875", "2762", "2930", "2931", "2939", "3481", "3483", "34831", "34839", "78001", "78009", "99592")

hospitalization = data.table(hospitalization)

##
# OK, now the operations only take a few lines:

#Make a column called "organ function" which is the sum of 3 logical tests
# Logical values are coerced to 0 and 1, so you get the count across the diagnoses
hospitalization = hospitalization %>%
  mutate(organ_function = diagnosis1 %in% organ_dysfunction + diagnosis2 %in% organ_dysfunction +diagnosis3 %in% organ_dysfunction)

# Summarize, counting all the rows in subsets divided up
# by the number of dysfunction counts.  Note that n() gives row count.
dysfunction_counts = hospitalization %>%
  group_by(organ_function) %>%
  summarize(no_cases = n())
